title: A Pluto year

sections.heading: One slow lap
paragraphs: Earth goes around the Sun once each year. Pluto takes about 248 Earth years. That is nearly 250 birthdays for one trip! Pluto is a small, icy world with a very big clock.

sections.heading: A new start
paragraphs: In 1776, thirteen colonies declared that they were free from Britain. The United States was born. People dreamed of freedom. But enslaved people were still not free. There was much more work to do.

sections.heading: So much in one lap
paragraphs: America’s first 250 years span just over one Pluto year. In that time came the Civil War, then World War I and World War II. Think of your parents. Then their parents. Then their parents! Many groups of children grew up and raised children of their own.

sections.heading: One more jump back
paragraphs: Go back 250 years before 1776. You land in 1526. In India, Babur began the Mughal Empire. He also loved gardens. People were building things that others would see long after they were gone.

sections.heading: What was in a pocket?
paragraphs: In 1776, people used coins and paper money. Now we can also pay with cards and phones. Bitcoin is digital money. You cannot hold it in your hand. What might people use 250 years from now?

sections.heading: A gift for tomorrow
paragraphs: Imagine giving a child a gold coin. Then imagine that gift passing from one child to the next. Would it still buy something after a Pluto year? What about a dollar? Or Bitcoin? We do not know what any of them will be worth. I’m grateful for the people who helped build the world we share. What can we leave for the children still to come?

transcript: Hey explorers! Can two worlds help us draw? Mercury, the closest planet to the Sun, goes around in about 88 Earth days. Far away Pluto is a dwarf planet. One trip takes about 248 Earth years. One Pluto year is about as long as the United States has existed. Mercury makes over a thousand trips, while Pluto makes one. Now, let's draw a line between them in our simple model. Keep each line as they move. Watch the thread spread. Look at that beautiful pattern! These lines are our drawing, not strings in space. What do you notice?

modelNotes.heading: Try the observation together
paragraphs: At one moment, mark both worlds and draw a joining line. Move forward by an equal time interval, mark both again, and keep the new line. Which marks show the paths, and which marks did you add? What happens when one world moves much faster? Describe what you notice before trying another starting position or drawing interval.

modelNotes.heading: What this illustration simplifies
paragraphs: The picture uses circular paths, constant angular speeds and compressed spacing and sizes. Real orbits are elliptical, and Pluto's orbit is inclined. Using JPL's listed sidereal periods gives approximately 1,029.37 Mercury orbits per Pluto orbit, rather than an exact integer loop. The spoken 88 days and 248 years are rounded figures. Starting positions are chosen for the illustration, not calculated historical positions.

modelNotes.heading: How the threads are sampled
paragraphs: The drawing spans 1,600 equal time intervals over one modeled Pluto orbit, with 1,601 sampled positions including both endpoints, about 56.6 Earth days apart. The pattern depends on that interval and the starting positions; it does not promise a particular flower or exact closure. The drawing uses a fine-line lattice with a cycling color palette. Line weight and color are illustration choices. Fast Mercury is represented by a trail during the accelerated reveal to avoid a misleading slow strobing dot. The joining lines are drawing marks, not physical connections or orbital tracks.
